newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Telstra may join global telecoms alliance.
newsitem.headline: Telstra may join global telecoms alliance.

text.p: Australia's leading telecommunications company, Telstra Corp, said on Monday it was negotiating entry into a global telecommunications alliance.

Telstra's chief executive office, Frank Blount, told a news conference in Singapore the world had changed over the last few years and it was necessary to join to join a strong global partnership of fellow telecommunications players.
Blount refused to say which of the three giant global alliances -- Global One, World Partners and Concert -- Telstra was talking about joining.
Concert is an alliance lead by British Telecom and MCI of the United States. Global One groups France Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and Sprint of the United States.
World Partners is a loose alliance led by AT&T.
Blount said Telstra had held back from declaring its hand to see how the world telecoms market was developing.

"I think the time is coming when we need to declare ourselves," Blount said. "The time has come for us to join one." Asked by reporters when the government-owned group would make an announcement, Blount replied; "As soon as we can get the right deal done."
He said declined to say how far negotiations had gone and would not say whether World Partners, to which Telstra is now affiliated, was the most likely option.
He said Telstra would prefer to swap some equity with its new partners.
"I would prefer equity held," he said.
Blount said Telstra's attitude to joining an alliance because barriers to global investment in the telecoms industry were falling rapidly.

"The reason it is time to join is because I think it is becoming much clearer now in the last year, year and a half, what is happening in the global telecoms game ... and because of liberalisation of most markets around the world," he said.
"Things have changed in the last few years."
Blount earlier told the Asia Telecom 97 trade fair in Singapore that the future telecoms industry would not be dominated by monolithic monopoly players, but probably by looser alliances.
"I'm not proposing mega-mergers," he told the news conference.
